LPH completed an electrical system check of the home. During the inspection, we evaluated the electrical panel and breakers, visible wiring and connections, switches and receptacles, GFCI protection, exterior electrical devices, smoke and carbon monoxide detection, and overall visible safety and operating conditions of the electrical system.

Bathroom Exhaust Fan / GFCI Investigation:
LPH also investigated a reported issue with the bathroom exhaust fan causing the GFCI to trip when the fan is turned off. The homeowner reported that this has only occurred twice. Due to the limited number of occurrences, there is currently not enough evidence to confirm a consistent electrical fault.

LPH pulled the wiring down at the fan and inspected the wiring and connections at the fan, switch box, and GFCI. We verified that the wiring was properly positioned and that no conductors were touching where they should not. During our inspection, nothing was found that would cause immediate concern or indicate an obvious ground fault.

The wiring has been inspected and repositioned as necessary in an effort to eliminate the possibility of an unintended ground fault at the connections. We are hopeful this resolves the issue. However, because the GFCI trip has occurred specifically when the fan is being turned off, there is also a possibility that the fan motor may be contributing to the occasional trip.

As a motor ages, small amounts of electrical leakage can potentially develop. When power to a motor is interrupted, the magnetic energy stored within the motor can also create a brief electrical transient. In some circumstances, this can result in a momentary current imbalance that a sensitive GFCI detects and responds to by tripping. Since this has only happened twice and no visible wiring problem was found, LPH recommends monitoring the fan for now. If the GFCI continues to trip, further troubleshooting may be necessary, including evaluation of the fan motor and potentially replacing the fan if it is determined to be the source of the issue.

Four-Way Switch – Arcing:
One four-way switch was found to be arcing when being turned on and off. Arcing can create excessive heat at the switch connection and can eventually damage the device or surrounding wiring. LPH recommends replacing the switch to restore a secure electrical connection and prevent continued arcing.

Exterior Receptacles – Corrosion:
Three exterior receptacles were found to be corroded from exposure to outdoor moisture and weather conditions. LPH recommends replacing these devices with weather-resistant receptacles designed to better withstand the outdoor environment and provide improved long-term reliability.

Mechanical Room Smoke/Carbon Monoxide Detector:
The combination smoke and carbon monoxide detector located in the mechanical room with the furnace is over 20 years old. Smoke/CO detectors have a limited service life, and their operation should not be relied upon once they are past their recommended service period. LPH recommends replacing this detector with a new combination smoke and carbon monoxide detector to provide reliable detection in an area containing the home’s heating equipment.

Panel Breakers – Shared Neutral Concern:
LPH found two tandem 20-amp breakers serving circuits that are sharing a neutral in a configuration that presents a safety concern. The associated circuit conductors need to be properly configured so the circuits can be safely disconnected together when required. LPH recommends replacing the two existing tandem breakers with the appropriate 20-amp quad tandem breaker to provide proper circuit disconnecting and maintain safe operation of the circuits.

LPH reviewed the electrical system findings and recommended corrections with the homeowner. The recommended work is intended to address the identified safety concerns, improve reliability, and update aging or deteriorated electrical components.

After reviewing the electrical system with the homeowner, LPH’s only recommendations are the following GFCI protection upgrades:

1. GFCI Protection – Washing Machine

LPH recommends installing GFCI protection for the washing machine receptacle. The washing machine is located in an area where water supply hoses, drain connections, or the appliance itself could potentially leak or become loose. If water were to reach the electrical wiring or components, it could create an unintended path for electrical current.

In certain fault conditions, energized wiring contacting water or the metal housing of the appliance could allow voltage to transfer onto the appliance housing, creating a potential shock hazard. GFCI protection is designed to quickly detect this type of unintended current path and shut the circuit off, providing an additional layer of protection for anyone who may come into contact with the appliance.

2. GFCI Protection – Garbage Disposal

LPH also recommends installing GFCI protection for the garbage disposal receptacle located underneath the kitchen sink. This is a moisture-prone location because the receptacle and disposal wiring are located near the sink’s water supply, drain plumbing, and disposal connections.

If a plumbing connection were to leak or come loose, water could reach the receptacle, wiring, or electrical components. GFCI protection provides additional protection by quickly disconnecting power if current begins traveling along an unintended path, helping reduce the potential for electrical shock or an energized appliance housing.

These recommendations are proactive safety upgrades rather than indications that the home’s electrical system is currently in poor condition. With the remainder of the electrical system found to be in fantastic shape, these upgrades would provide additional protection specifically at two locations where water and electrical equipment are in close proximity.

3. Whole-Home Surge Protection

LPH recommends adding a whole-home surge protection device at the electrical panel to provide an additional layer of protection for the home’s electrical system and connected electronics.

Electrical surges can come from outside sources, such as lightning strikes or utility-related events, but many smaller surges are actually generated inside the home when motor-driven equipment cycles on and off. Appliances and equipment such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washing machines, dryers, and garage door openers can create these smaller electrical disturbances.

Modern electronics are particularly sensitive to these fluctuations because many appliances and devices contain electronic control boards, circuit boards, power supplies, and LED drivers. A surge protector installed at the main electrical panel helps divert excessive voltage away from the home’s branch circuits and connected equipment, providing protection throughout the home rather than relying solely on individual plug-in surge protectors.

This is a proactive protection upgrade, not an indication that the electrical system is currently experiencing a problem. With the home’s electrical system otherwise found to be in fantastic condition, whole-home surge protection provides an added level of protection for the investment the homeowner has in their appliances, electronics, and electrical equipment.

Dryer Electrical Safety Issue

The homeowner reported receiving an electrical shock when touching the dryer while also making contact with another grounded surface. LPH investigated the dryer circuit and initially confirmed that the receptacle and connections at the wall were properly installed.

LPH then pulled the dryer away from the wall and inspected the electrical connection compartment on the appliance. During this inspection, we discovered a serious wiring and grounding issue at the dryer itself. The cable entering the dryer was not secured with a proper connector, and the conductors had been terminated incorrectly.

The dryer had been wired with the hot conductors connected to the incorrect terminals, including a hot conductor being connected to the dryer’s neutral connection and the neutral conductor being connected to one of the primary hot connections. Additionally, the dryer was designed to operate using a 4-wire configuration, which requires the neutral and equipment grounding conductor to remain electrically separated. Instead, the neutral conductor had been improperly bonded to the metal housing of the dryer.

This configuration created a significant shock hazard because the metal chassis of the dryer could become energized. LPH identified this condition as the likely cause of the homeowner’s reported shock.

Dryer Wiring Correction

LPH corrected the dryer wiring to restore the appliance to the proper 4-wire configuration. This included:

* Removing the improperly installed cable connection and installing a proper strain-relief/connector where the wiring enters the dryer.
* Correctly identifying and terminating both hot conductors on their proper terminals.
* Correctly terminating the neutral conductor on the dryer’s neutral connection.
* Removing the improper neutral-to-ground bond from the dryer housing.
* Installing the equipment grounding conductor onto the dryer’s designated bonding/grounding connection.
* Verifying that the neutral and equipment grounding paths were properly separated as required for a 4-wire dryer installation.
* Testing the corrected installation to confirm proper electrical operation and safety.

After the repair, LPH had the homeowner operate the dryer with a wet towel load to verify proper operation under normal conditions and confirm that the appliance was functioning correctly following the wiring correction. The dryer operated properly, and no additional issues were identified during testing.

Downstairs Bedroom Bathroom Switch

LPH also identified an arcing single-pole switch in the downstairs bedroom bathroom. The switch was replaced to eliminate the arcing condition and restore safe, reliable operation.

Whole-Home Surge Protection

As an additional protection option, LPH installed a Type 1 whole-home surge protective device directly underneath the main service lugs. This provides the home with an additional layer of protection against damaging voltage surges that can enter through the electrical service and potentially affect sensitive electronics, appliances, and electrical equipment throughout the home.

LPH tested and confirmed proper operation of all completed installations and corrections.

The primary concern identified during today’s inspection was the improperly wired dryer, which presented a significant electrical shock hazard. LPH completed a thorough electrical system check throughout the home, including an evaluation of the main electrical service, meter base, service entrance conductors, electrical panel, breakers, grounding and bonding, wiring, receptacles, switches, GFCI/AFCI protection, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, visible junction boxes and connections, and the overall condition and operation of the home’s electrical equipment. LPH also checked for visible signs of overheating, corrosion, moisture intrusion, damaged or deteriorated components, improper wiring, and other conditions that could affect the safety, reliability, or proper operation of the electrical system.

The remainder of the home’s electrical system has been fully updated and is currently in great working order. LPH did not identify any significant concerns with the updated portions of the electrical system during today’s evaluation. The primary concern identified is with the aging exterior electrical service and evidence of moisture intrusion and corrosion associated with the existing service entrance.

Outside Service Replacement – Corrosion & Moisture Intrusion

LPH found visible corrosion where the neutral conductor exits the protective jacket as it enters the main electrical panel. The majority of the interior panel is clean, with rust staining concentrated at the base of the panel directly below where the service cable enters. This is an indication that moisture may be entering through the compromised service entrance rather than originating from within the panel itself.

LPH inspected the existing exterior meter base and found it to be an older, obsolete model that is showing its age. After removing the cover, a significant amount of rust buildup was observed inside the meter base, including corrosion around the meter lugs where the service entrance conductors are secured. The existing sealing at the top of the meter base is also old and deteriorated and may have provided an additional point of water entry.

A small tear was also identified in the upper portion of the service entrance cable. This creates another potential pathway for water to enter the cable jacket. Although the exposed portions of the neutral conductor inside the meter base appear relatively clean where they are able to dry, the greater concern is moisture becoming trapped inside the cable jacket where it can remain against the conductors and promote continued corrosion. Additional damage may also be present within the cable that cannot be fully evaluated until the existing cable is removed and dropped.

The neutral conductor is critical to maintaining proper voltage distribution throughout the home. If corrosion continues to weaken the neutral connection and the neutral were to fail, the home’s electrical system could experience an unstable or unbalanced voltage condition. This can result in some circuits receiving significantly more voltage than intended while others receive less, potentially causing serious damage to electronics, appliances, lighting, and other electrical equipment. Due to the visible corrosion, moisture concerns, aging meter base, deteriorated sealing, and compromised service cable, LPH recommends replacing the outside service before the condition can continue to deteriorate.

Complete Outside Service Replacement

LPH will remove the existing outside service and install a new code-compliant 100-amp exterior service. This will include:

* Removal of the existing obsolete meter base and outside service equipment.
* Cutting a new opening in the siding as needed to properly accommodate the new meter base.
* Installation of a new code-compliant 100-amp meter base.
* Installation of new service conductors protected within PVC conduit to protect them from future physical wear and weather exposure.
* Properly strapping the conduit to the home.
* Installation of a new PVC service head.
* Installation of a new code-compliant exterior emergency disconnect.
* Installation of new wiring from the meter base to the exterior disconnect.
* Continuation of the protected conduit run to the point where the service enters the basement.
* Installation of a new bonding bridge at the exterior service equipment.
* Relocation and lengthening of the grounding conductors as needed to properly terminate at the new exterior disconnect.
* Separation of the neutral and grounding conductors within the existing panel as required for the new service configuration.
* Proper bonding and grounding of the new service equipment.
* Sealing the new meter base and disconnect with silicone to help prevent future water intrusion.
* Sealing the service entrance where the new conduit and conductors enter the home.

This replacement will eliminate the compromised section of the existing service cable and replace the aging exterior equipment with a properly protected and weather-resistant service configuration. The new installation will significantly reduce the opportunity for future physical damage and water penetration while providing a safer, more reliable, and code-compliant outside service.

Technician was shown the electrical breaker panel and the location of the well pump and pressure tank outside in the well house. Upon inspection of the well house, Technician noticed the door was left wide open and the pressure tank was tipped over. Technician repositioned the pressure tank into an upright position and secured it so it is sitting flat and cannot tip over.

Technician then inspected the electrical panel and found the existing Square D Homeline 15-amp double-pole breaker in the off/tripped position. Technician turned the breaker on and checked the voltage entering the pressure switch, which measured approximately 244 VAC.

Technician ran water from the boiler drain to operate the well pump and checked the pump’s electrical readings. The well pump was drawing approximately 5.19–5.26 amps and tested at approximately 6.9 ohms for continuity. These readings indicate the well pump is operating properly.

Technician then checked the continuity of the existing well wire from the electrical panel to the pressure switch. The expected resistance should be approximately 0–0.5 ohms; however, the existing well wire measured approximately 12–14 ohms. These readings indicate the existing well wire is compromised and should be replaced.

The existing Square D Homeline 15-amp double-pole breaker should also be replaced with a properly sized Square D Homeline double-pole breaker.

Technician recommends replacing the existing underground well wire from the electrical panel to the pressure switch. Technician will trench a new path for the well wire from the electrical panel located in the bedroom to the well house, approximately 60 feet away. New electrical conduit will be installed to provide additional protection for the new well wire. Technician will also replace the existing 15-amp double-pole breaker with a 30-amp double-pole breaker.

The findings indicate the compromised well wire and tripped breaker are the reason for the loss of water. Technician also determined that the pressure tank being tipped over is likely related to groundwater rising inside the well house. The increased water level can cause the pressure tank to become buoyant and potentially cause the pressure switch to come into contact with water.

With the replacement of the well wire, Technician recommends relocating the pressure tank and electrical pressure switch higher on the plywood wall inside the well house. This will help keep the electrical components and pressure tank above potential groundwater levels and reduce the risk of future water exposure.

Technician will need to remove a portion of the drywall around the electrical panel in the bedroom to complete the electrical work. LPH is not responsible for drywall repairs or landscaping restoration following completion of the installation.

Technician attempted to contact the homeowner multiple times to provide an update regarding the findings and condition of the well pump system, as well as the applicable dispatch fee. Technician was unable to reach the homeowner and left a message.

During today’s electrical system evaluation, LPH identified extensive evidence of water intrusion and resulting corrosion affecting multiple components of the underground electrical service, including the exterior meter base and interior electrical panel.

The exterior meter base has a film of corrosion present across the meter base lugs and neutral bar, with corrosion visible throughout the affected components. The meter base also shows evidence that water has entered the enclosure and collected in the bottom.

Additional evidence of water entry was found at the interior electrical panel. Corrosion is present along the top portion of the panel, with dried drip marks extending down the interior of the enclosure and along the conductors leading to the breakers. A dried water stain is also present where water appears to have previously pooled on top of the two breakers located at the upper portion of the panel. Rust is present on several breaker screws, along with additional rust spots on the panel enclosure and cover.

The paper circuit labeling inside the panel and on the panel cover shows significant evidence of having been exposed to moisture. Portions of the paper have visible water damage, and mold has formed on the affected labeling. Several copper conductors connected to breakers also have small areas of green oxidation consistent with moisture exposure.

LPH compared today’s findings with the electrical system inspection performed last year. These conditions were not documented during the previous inspection. Based on the extent and pattern of the corrosion, dried drip marks, water staining, oxidation, and other evidence present throughout the service equipment, the damage appears to have occurred more recently than the previous inspection.

Safety Concerns

The extent of the water-related damage makes this a serious electrical safety concern. Electrical equipment is designed to operate in a dry environment, and moisture inside service equipment can contribute to corrosion, deterioration of electrical connections, increased electrical resistance, overheating, arcing, breaker malfunction, and failure of electrical components.

Of particular concern is that evidence of moisture is present at multiple points within the electrical service rather than being isolated to a single component. Water has affected the meter base, service equipment, panel enclosure, breakers, wiring, and electrical connections. Continued operation of equipment with this level of moisture-related deterioration creates an increased risk of electrical malfunction and further damage.

Because some of the affected components are part of the home’s primary electrical service, the concern extends beyond an individual receptacle or branch circuit. The service equipment is responsible for safely distributing electrical power throughout the home, making the condition of these components especially important.

Recommended Corrective Work

Due to the considerable evidence of water intrusion affecting multiple components of the electrical service, LPH recommends replacing the affected service equipment and associated wiring to restore the system to a safe, properly protected, and code-compliant condition.

The recommended service replacement would include:

* Required electrical inspections and coordination of the electrical service shutdown.
* Removal of the existing exterior meter base and installation of a new meter base.
* Proper sealing of the new meter base to help prevent future water intrusion.
* Installation of a new exterior emergency disconnect.
* Installation of new conduit from the exterior disconnect into the home.
* Sealing of the disconnect, meter base, conduit, and all electrical entry points into the home.
* Reconfiguration of the interior panel as a subpanel, with the grounding system properly established at the service disconnect.
* Installation of the required bonding bridge.
* Installation of new four-wire conductors from the exterior disconnect to the interior panel.
* Installation of whole-home surge protection.
* Removal of the existing water-affected interior panel and associated equipment.
* Installation of a new 42-space Eaton CH loadcenter.
* Proper relocation and termination of the existing branch-circuit wiring into the new panel.
* Complete circuit identification and relabeling of the new panel.
* Installation of any additional grounding required by applicable code.
* Completion of all required inspections.
* Full electrical testing following completion to verify proper operation of the electrical system and connected components.

The recommended replacement will remove the water-affected electrical equipment from service and provide a new, properly sealed service assembly. It will also allow the grounding, bonding, disconnect, feeder, and panel configuration to be established correctly as part of the replacement.

Because the previous inspection did not document these conditions and today’s inspection identified significant evidence of more recent water intrusion, LPH recommends that the homeowner retain this evaluation, photographs, and estimate as documentation of the condition found.

Due to the seriousness of the electrical conditions observed, LPH recommends addressing the affected service equipment rather than continuing to rely on electrical components showing significant evidence of moisture exposure and corrosion.

As a separate recommendation LPH found that the two existing exterior receptacles are not weather resistant and one that is in a direct rain area has an improper cover. We recommended replacing these with new weather-resistant receptacles designed for outdoor use. The existing receptacles are rated for indoor use and have corrosion buildup inside the devices where the electrical plug makes contact.

Corrosion at the contact points can prevent the plug from making a clean, secure electrical connection. This increased resistance can cause heat to build up when the receptacle is under load, potentially leading to discoloration, overheating, arcing, or premature failure of the device. Because these receptacles are located outdoors, continued exposure to moisture can accelerate the corrosion and increase the potential for electrical problems.

LPH will also replace the existing gray cover outdoor cover with a properly rated wet-location, extra-duty in-use bubble cover on the back porch. The cover will remain closed over the receptacle and plugged-in device, helping prevent rain and moisture from reaching the electrical connections while the receptacle is in use. The box and cover will be properly sealed to provide additional protection against water intrusion.

The new weather-resistant receptacles and properly rated covers will provide a safer, more durable connection point for outdoor use and help protect the electrical devices from moisture and corrosion.

We were called out to evaluate why the home’s electric was not functioning correctly. Upon arrival, we spoke with Eugene to identify his main concerns and the location of his concerns. Eugene stated that when he would run his microwave, it would bog down pretty heavy and affect the lights in the kitchen. He also stated that his fridge in the basement would do the same thing and he wanted to know what was going on. We did a thorough evaluation starting at the main electrical panel where we assessed irregular voltage readings at the main breaker and at each individual breaker from this point. We received 128 V from one phase to neutral and 110 V from the other phase to neutral. We then had Eugene start his microwave and immediately noticed that the same phase the microwave was on, dropped to 110 V while the other phase spiked past 130V. This leads us to the conclusion that the neutral wire feeding this house is bad. We then began to search where the neutral wire has failed, whether it was PPL’s powerline or the homeowners service wire (that was older and brittle) on the home. After a thorough evaluation, we discovered that the neutral wire on the homeowner side of the connection is bad and received the same irregular voltages, as when we tested inside the main panel. We confirmed this by testing PPL voltage while under load and when the power is turned off, and the voltage was steady during both instances. We provided multiple solutions to remedy the exterior service wire but also provided option options to replace the electrical panel whether it’s the 100 amp counterparts or the 200 amp upgrade. Eugene opted to go with the 100 amp replacement prior to leaving today. We also re-crimped the neutral wire today to allow the home to function correctly until we can come back and replace the entire wire. After doing so the voltages were reading normal even during a heavier load. We thank you for trusting us to evaluate your electrical concern and provide solutions to remedy this concern.
